title: Helka_Lab_4
text:
Code
library(glmmTMB)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom.mixed)
library(performance)
library(gt)
library(readr)
library(DHARMa)
library(ggeffects)
library(titanic)

titanic <- titanic_train




Code
titanic <- titanic |>
  select(Survived, Sex, Age, Pclass) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    Sex.Binary = case_when(
      Sex == "male" ~ 0,
      Sex == "female" ~ 1)) |>
  mutate(
    Survived.Char = case_when(
      Survived == 0 ~ "Died",
      Survived == 1 ~ "Survived")) |>
  mutate(
    Pclass.Char = case_when(
      Pclass == "1" ~ "First Class",
      Pclass == "2" ~ "Second Class",
      Pclass == "3" ~ "Third Class")) |>
  mutate(Pclass = factor(Pclass, levels = c(1, 2, 3))) |>
  select(Survived, Survived.Char, Sex, Sex.Binary, Pclass, Pclass.Char, Age)
 
n <- nrow(titanic)


The data set contains information about 714 Titanic passengers and whether they survived or died in the Titanic crash (Survived), their sex reported on legal documents (Sex), their self reported age (Age), and type of ticket purchasesed which can be a proxy for socoioeconomic status (Pclass).


How are Sex, Age, and Pclass associated with whether a passenger Survived the crash?
I expect:

Passengers who were female were more likely to survive the crash due to the rule of women and children first into the lifeboats.
Passengers with lower Age were more likely to survive the crash due to the rule of women and children first into the lifeboats.
Passengers with lower Pclass were more likely to survive the crash because higher status would be higher on deck and able to reach the lifeboats faster while also being prioritized. (Please note that lower Pclass is associated with a more expensive ticket)

These are predictions about associations, not causal effects.








Code
age_stats <- titanic |>
  summarise(
    across(
      Age,
      list(mean = mean, sd = sd, min = min, max = max)
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = c("variable", ".value"),
    names_sep = "_"
  )

age_stats |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = where(is.numeric), decimals = 2)

The average age of passengers was 29.7 years (SD = 14.53), with ages ranging from 0.42 to 80 years. This suggests that the sample included a relatively wide age range, although passengers tended to be younger adults in their late 20’s on average.





Code
survival_counts <- titanic |>
  count(Survived.Char) 

survival_counts|>
  gt()








Survived.Char
n

Survived

More passengers died (424) than survived (290), indicating that survival outcomes were not evenly distributed. This is expectedsince this historic tragedy was known for a large death count and a small survival rate.





Code
sex_counts <- titanic |>
  count(Sex) 

sex_counts |>
  gt()








Sex
n




female

The sample included 453 males and 261 females, indicating an uneven distribution, with males representing the larger proportion of passengers. This is also to be expected since women had less rights when the Titanic sunk and would not have traveled alone, unlike men.





Code
class_counts <- titanic |>
  count(Pclass.Char) 

class_counts |>
  gt()








Pclass.Char
n




First Class
186


Second Class
173


Third Class
355







Passenger class was also unevenly distributed, with Third Class having the most passengers (355), followed by First Class (186) and Second Class (173). I expected Third Class to have the largest sample size as there are often more lower class citizen’s in a society than upper class citizen’s. What was surprising is that First Class had a larger number of passengers than Second Class but by a much smaller amount.
Overall, all of the categorical variable are unevenly distributed between groups. As unequal counts can influence the values of coefficients and statistical signiciance (as larger sample sizes result in higher precision values and a greater chance to find a significant effect) I will need to consider the difference in sample sizes when interpreting my results.

title: Helka_Lab_4
section: Part 2: Specify and estimate competing models
text:
Part 2: Specify and estimate competing models


Code
mod0 <- glmmTMB(Survived ~ 1,data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

mod1 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex.Binary,
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

mod2 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex.Binary + Pclass,
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))

mod3 <- glmmTMB(
  Survived ~ Sex.Binary + Pclass + Age,
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"))




Code
#summary(mod0)
#summary(mod1)
#summary(mod2)
#summary(mod3)

confint(mod3)


                  2.5 %      97.5 %    Estimate
(Intercept)  0.54886723  1.95959737  1.25423230
Sex.Binary   2.11630257  2.92925952  2.52278104
Pclass2     -1.85479161 -0.76480625 -1.30979893
Pclass3     -3.13223077 -2.02901928 -2.58062502
Age         -0.05199065 -0.02197992 -0.03698528


As can be seen in the Confidence Interval Output, all of the coefficients are statistically significant (p < 0.001) in the third model, and this was seen throughout the different models. Practically speaking, the log-odds of survival decreased the most between First and Third Class, with an estimated coefficient of -2.58, and increased between males and females, with an estimated coefficient of 2.52.
Furthermore, the intercept continously changes as additional predictors are added. Between mod0 and mod1 where Sex is added in, the intercept decreases as sex explained the variation between men and women and their probability of survival with the intercept reflecting the probability of a man surviving which is lower than a female. Then for mod2, Pclass further explains variation in the data where chance of survival decreases and so the intercept, although still negative, was larger than mod1. This showed the probability of a male in first class’s chance at survival which was higher than the other classes but still lower than a female’s probability of survival. Finally, in mod3 the intercept becomes positive. This is because, age further explained a decreased probability of survivial. The intercept in mod3 reflected a newborn, first class, male’s survival rate which was relatively high.

text:
Part 3: Nested Model Comparisons

Nested-model χ²-tests


Code
tests <- anova(mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3)

tests


Data: titanic
Models:
mod0: Survived ~ 1, zi=~0, disp=~1
mod1: Survived ~ Sex.Binary, zi=~0, disp=~1
mod2: Survived ~ Sex.Binary + Pclass, zi=~0, disp=~1
mod3: Survived ~ Sex.Binary + Pclass + Age, zi=~0, disp=~1
     Df    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance   Chisq Chi Df Pr(>Chisq)    
mod0  1 966.52 971.09 -482.26   964.52                              
mod1  2 754.70 763.84 -375.35   750.70 213.816      1  < 2.2e-16 ***
mod2  4 680.43 698.71 -336.22   672.43  78.269      2  < 2.2e-16 ***
mod3  5 657.28 680.14 -323.64   647.28  25.148      1  5.311e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




Code
tests <- tests |>
   select(Chisq, Df, `Chi Df`, `Pr(>Chisq)`) |>
   rename(
     Nested.df = `Chi Df`,
     Nested.Chisq.stat = Chisq,
     Nested.p.value = `Pr(>Chisq)`,
     model.df = Df) 

tests


     Nested.Chisq.stat model.df Nested.df Nested.p.value
mod0                          1                         
mod1           213.816        2         1     0.0000e+00
mod2            78.269        4         2     0.0000e+00
mod3            25.148        5         1     5.3106e-07


Code
sex_test <- tests["mod1", ]
class_test <- tests["mod2", ]
age_test <- tests["mod3", ]


The ANOVA results indicate that each successive model significantly improved model fit. Adding Sex to the intercept-only model significantly improved fit, χ²(1) = 213.816, p < .001. Similarly, adding Pclass significantly improved fit beyond Sex alone, χ²(2) = 78.269, p < .001. Finally, adding Age also significantly improved fit beyond the model containing Sex and Pclass, χ²(1) = 25.148, p < .001. These findings are further supported by the decreasing AIC and BIC values and increasing log-likelihood across the four models, suggesting that the additional predictors improve model fit even after accounting for model complexity.


Extract overall model performance


Code
glance0 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod0)
glance1 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod1)
glance2 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod2)
glance3 <- broom.mixed::glance(mod3)




Code
mods <- c(
  "mod0: Null",
  "mod1: Sex",
  "mod2: + PClass",
  "mod3: + Age")

glances <- rbind(
  glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2,
  glance3)




Combine nested tests and model performance


Code
comparison_table <- cbind(
  Model = mods,
  glances,
  tests)

  select(
    Model,
    AIC,
    BIC,
    logLik,
    deviance,
    df.residual,
    Nested.df,
    Nested.Chisq.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    AIC = "AIC",
    BIC = "BIC",
    logLik = "Log-likelihood",
    deviance = "Deviance",
    df.residual = "Residual.df",

    columns = c(

Interpreting the combined table
Model 3 provides the best fit to the data, as it has the lowest AIC (657.28) and BIC (680.14), suggesting that the improvement in model fit justifies the additional complexity. The likelihood-ratio tests also indicate that each addition significantly improves model fit: Sex had a χ² of 213.82 (p < .001), Pclass had a χ² of 78.27 (p < .001), and Age had a χ² of 25.15 (p < .001). Therefore, AIC and BIC support the same general conclusion as the likelihood-ratio tests, as all three measures indicate that adding predictors improves the model. Overall, these results suggest that Sex makes the largest contribution to improving model fit, followed by Pclass and Age, although all three predictors provide statistically significant improvements.

title: Helka_Lab_4
section: Part 4: Evaluate Binary logistic regression diagnostics
text:
Part 4: Evaluate Binary logistic regression diagnostics

Selecting the Model


Code
selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  filter(Nested.p.value < .05) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1)


selected_name <- selected_row$Model

selected_model <- switch(
  selected_name,
  "mod0: Null" = mod0,
  "mod1: Sex" = mod1,
  "mod2: + PClass" = mod2,
  "mod3: + Age" = mod3)


The provisionally selected model is mod3: + Age.
Its performance is:

AIC = 657.283
BIC = 680.138

I will now examine whether the selected model has important diagnostic problems.



Evaluate binary logistic regression diagnostics

Linearity on the logit scale


Code
set.seed(9041)
res_mod3 <- simulateResiduals(mod3, n = 500, plot = FALSE)




The default DHARMa plot









The QQ plot showed residuals closely following the expected reference line, with nonsignificant KS (p = .903), dispersion (p = .812), and outlier (p = .541) tests. Although some slight curvature was visible in the residuals versus predicted values plot, the combined adjusted quantile test was not significant. Overall, these results suggest no substantial evidence of residual distribution or dispersion problems.


Collinearity


# Check for Multicollinearity

Low Correlation

       Term  VIF   VIF 95% CI adj. VIF Tolerance Tolerance 95% CI
 Sex.Binary 1.07 [1.02, 1.23]     1.04      0.93     [0.81, 0.98]
     Pclass 1.42 [1.30, 1.57]     1.09      0.71     [0.64, 0.77]
        Age 1.33 [1.23, 1.48]     1.15      0.75     [0.68, 0.81]


All VIF values were relatively low, ranging from 1.07 to 1.42, while tolerance values ranged from 0.71 to 0.93. These results suggest that multicollinearity is not a concern and that the predictors provide distinct information towards predicting the probability of a passenger surviving the Titanic.


Complete separation
Complete separation was assessed by examining the model coefficients and standard errors in the r console using:
r summary(mod3)
Neither the coefficient estimates or standard errors appear too large or infinite which suggests that there is no obvious evidence of complete separation so the predictors do not perfectly distinguish between survival outcomes.


Influence


Code
testOutliers(res_mod3)










    DHARMa outlier test based on exact binomial test with approximate
    expectations

data:  res_mod3
outliers at both margin(s) = 1, observations = 714, p-value = 0.5412
alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.003992016
95 percent confidence interval:
 3.545849e-05 7.778486e-03
sample estimates:
frequency of outliers (expected: 0.00399201596806387 ) 
                                            0.00140056 


The DHARMa outlier test results were not statistically significant (p = .541), suggesting no evidence of an unusually high number of outlying observations. Furthermore, the resulting plot shows no signs of outliers.


Events per predictor
Here we have 290 survivors and 424 deceased passengers, with 5 coefficients in mod3. This means there were 58 survivor events per coefficient and 84.8 deceased passenger events per coefficient. Both of these values are sufficient number of events per predictor.
Overall, the diagnostic findings support using mod3 as the selected model.

section: Part 5: Selecting and Reporting my Model
text:
Part 5: Selecting and Reporting my Model

Selecting the Model
I am selecting Model 3 as my preferred model. The nested-model χ²-tests indicated that each additional predictor significantly improved model fit which was mirroed by the significant p-values for each of the additional variables. Model 3 also had the lowest AIC and BIC, demonstrating that even after accounting for model complexity it still explained more variance in the data. The diagnostic findings also supported its suitability, with no concerns identified regarding collinearity, residual distribution, complete separation, or events per predictor. Overall, even though Model 3 includes more parameters, the improvements in fit justify the additional complexity; especially since the four variables can be easily explained ensuring the model can still be understood and interpreted.

Interpret the results

Interpretting coefficients on the log-odds scale


Code
fixef(mod3)



Conditional model:
(Intercept)   Sex.Binary      Pclass2      Pclass3          Age  
    1.25423      2.52278     -1.30980     -2.58063     -0.03699  


The coefficients represent changes in the log-odds of survival, holding the other predictors constant.
The coefficient for Sex.Binary represents the log-odds difference between males and females, holding class and age constant. Male is the reference group, therefore the log-odds of surviving increases by 2.52 when the passenger is female versus male , holding class and avoidance constant.
The coefficient for PClass2 represents the log-odds difference between First Class and Second Class passengers, holding sex and age constant. First Class is the reference group, therefore the log-odds of surviving decreases by -1.31 when the passenger is second class versus first class, holding sex and age constant.
The coefficient for PClass3 represents the log-odds difference between First Class and Third Class passengers, holding sex and age constant. First Class is the reference group, therefore the log-odds of surviving decreases by -2.58 when the passenger is third class versus first class, holding sex and age constant.
For a one-point increase in age, holding sex and class constant, the log-odds of survival decrease by -0.04.


Interpretting transformed log-odds into odds ratios

Holding sex and class status constant, a one-year increase in age is associated with 0.96 times the odds of survival, 95% CI [0.95, 0.98].

Age

ggplot(pred_age, aes(x, predicted)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Age",
    y = "Predicted Probability of Survival"
  ) +
  theme_classic()

title: Helka_Lab_4
text:
Part 6: Results and Limitations

Results paragraph
I fit a binomial GLM with a logit link predicting Titanic survival probability from Sex, Class/Economic Status, and Age. Being female was associated with higher odds of survival compared to males, OR = 12.46, 95% CI [8.3, 18.71]. Second Class status was associated with lower odds of survival than First Class status, OR = 0.27, 95% CI [0.16, 0.47]. Third Class status was also associated with lower odds of survival than First Class status, OR = 0.08, 95% CI [0.04, 0.13]. Age was associated with lower odds of survival as it increased, OR = 0.96, 95% CI [0.95, 0.98].


Substantive conclusions and Limitation
This analysis illustrates how the probability of surviving the Titanic crash can be investigated using several competing binary logistic regression models.
The model-comparison process allows us to evaluate whether additional predictors explain meaningful variation beyond simpler models.
The final model provides estimates of the odds of a passenger surviving the Sinking of the Titanic. Female passengers were more likely to survive the sinking than male passengers. Younger passengers were also more likely to survive the sinking than older passengers. This aligns with the well-known rule of “Women and Children first” to evacuate in the case of an emergency. Finally, the higher class status one was, the higher probability of survival. This was also unsurprising as First Class passengers would have been both closer to the lifeboats and the rising water would reach them later, as their cabins were higher on the ship. They also would have been given priority to evacuate over lower class passengers.
There are two main limitations of this analysis. First, the data is observational and the results are strictly correlation so I cannot make any causal claims between passenger characteristics and survival probability. Second, the dataset contains a limited number of predictors, meaning that other factors could have been more significant in determining survival probability.
